note: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages, forgot what they had learned, and struggled to recall it. One asked whether their dead father knew of their anguish. The other answered from Job: His sons are honored yet he shall not know it. The first replied with the next verse, Only in his flesh does he feel pain, and Rabbi Yitzḥak's teaching that maggots hurt the dead like a needle in living flesh. They concluded that the dead know of their own pain but not of the pain of others.
why: The Gemara has just said the righteous are called living even in death and applied 'the dead know nothing' to the wicked; the brothers' exchange asks what the dead know, and the Gemara then challenges their answer with a story of spirits in a cemetery.

note: Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel in Yavne. Rabban Gamliel asked the Sages whether anyone knew how to compose the blessing against the heretics, and Shmuel HaKatan stood up and composed it. The next year, leading the prayer, he forgot it and spent two or three hours trying to recall it, and they did not remove him.
why: The Gemara has just asked why the prayer of eighteen blessings has nineteen, answering that the blessing of the heretics was added in Yavne; afterward it asks why Shmuel HaKatan was not removed, since a leader who errs in that blessing is suspected of heresy.

note: Ulla visited Rav Naḥman, ate, led Grace after Meals, and handed the cup of blessing to Rav Naḥman. Rav Naḥman asked him to send the cup to his wife Yalta. Ulla refused, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan that a woman's offspring are blessed only through her husband, from the verse: He will bless the fruit of your body. Yalta heard, rose in a rage, went into the wine store and broke four hundred barrels of wine. At Rav Naḥman's request Ulla sent her another cup with word that all the wine in the barrel was wine of blessing. She sent back: from peddlers, words, and from rags, lice.
why: The Gemara has just listed how the cup of blessing is handled, ending with sending it to one's household so one's wife will be blessed; Ulla's refusal disputes that last practice.
